title: Reading Real Code: Five Classic Bugs

chapters.title: Bug 1: a pointer to a dead local

scenes.say: An interviewer slides five short snippets across the table. Each hides one classic bug. By the end, you'll spot all five, and explain each like a senior engineer.
Read each snippet like a compiler, then like a memory diagram. Dangling pointers. Hidden copies. Vector growth. Three families, five bugs.
lines: Dangling pointers: a local, a freed int
Hidden copies: silent copies, double delete

scenes.title: Snippet one: what is wrong?
scenes.statement: getValue returns the address of its own local int. It compiles, and it might even print ten.
scenes.say: Snippet one looks innocent. Say we call getValue and print through the pointer. Undefined behavior, even if it prints ten.
Pause and decide. The function returns the address of x. Is that pointer safe to use after the call?
scenes.q: `int x = 10; return &x;` Is `*p` safe after the call?

scenes.head: Watch the stack
scenes.say: No: x is gone. Here's why. main calls getValue. Each call gets a stack frame, the memory for its locals. A new stack frame appears, with x holding ten. getValue returns its address, and p stores it. But the frame is popped the moment it returns. The next call reuses that memory. Reading star p is undefined: ten, garbage, or a crash.

scenes.head: The compiler warns, and fix one
scenes.say: Good news: the compiler warns. Read it. Fix one: return the int by value. Copying an int is free.

panels.label: fix one

output.text: warning: address of local variable ‘x’ returned [-Wreturn-local-addr]

scenes.head: Fix two: build it on the heap
scenes.say: Fix two: if it must outlive the call, build it on the heap, memory that lasts until you free it. A unique pointer owns that memory, and frees it for you.

scenes.title: Snippet two: what prints?
scenes.statement: Allocate an int holding five, delete it, then print through the pointer.

example.input: p = new int(5); delete p; cout << *p;

scenes.say: Three short lines. New int of five, delete p, print star p. Five, zero, or a crash? Use after free.
Make your call. What does the program print?
scenes.q: `int* p = new int(5); delete p; cout << *p;` Prints?

scenes.head: Delete does not touch p
scenes.say: Anything. Look at the heap. New makes a block holding five, and p holds its address. Delete hands the block back to the allocator. But p is unchanged: it still holds that address. The allocator may reuse the block, or write its own notes into it. Printing five proves nothing.

scenes.head: Catch it, then a band aid
scenes.say: Address Sanitizer, a memory checker built into the compiler, catches it at once and names it: heap use after free. A band aid: null the pointer after delete, so a later star p fails fast.

panels.label: bug
band aid

scenes.head: Make it impossible: make unique
scenes.say: But other copies still dangle. The real fix: make unique. No manual delete, and no way to touch freed memory.

panels.label: fix

scenes.title: Snippet three: count the prints
scenes.statement: A class prints in its constructor and its destructor. main makes a, then b from a. Count each line.
scenes.say: A counting puzzle. Test prints in its constructor and destructor. Take a, then b made from a. How many of each? One constructor, two destructors.
Pause and count. Two objects. How many Constructor lines, and how many Destructor lines?
scenes.q: `Test a; Test b = a;` Constructor / Destructor lines?

scenes.head: Count them live
scenes.say: One and two. Watch. Test a runs the default constructor: one Constructor line. Test b equals a is not your constructor. It's the copy constructor, which the compiler wrote, and it prints nothing. At the brace, b dies first, then a. Two objects, two destructors.

scenes.head: Make the copy visible
scenes.say: To see it, write the copy constructor yourself. Now the output shows every life: constructed, copied, and two destructions. Every object is destroyed once. Not every creation uses your constructor. And equals on an existing object is assignment.

scenes.title: Snippet four: is p still valid?
scenes.statement: Reserve room for two ints, push ten and twenty, and take a pointer to the first. Then push thirty.
scenes.say: A vector has room for two ints. Ten and twenty fill it. Pointer p aims at ten. Push thirty. Valid? No.
Pause and decide. The vector is full, and we push one more. Does p still point at ten?
scenes.q: Capacity 2, size 2, `int* p = &v[0]; v.push_back(30);` p valid?

scenes.head: The block moves
scenes.say: No. The vector is full, so push back allocates a bigger block, usually double. It moves ten and twenty across, adds thirty, and frees the old block. But p still holds the old address. It dangles.

scenes.head: The rule, and three fixes
scenes.say: The rule: if size would exceed capacity, every pointer, reference and iterator is invalidated. With spare room, only end is. Fix one: reserve enough before taking pointers. Fix two: keep an index, which survives growth. Fix three: take the pointer after the last push back.

scenes.title: Snippet five: the memory bug
scenes.statement: User allocates an int in its constructor, and deletes it in its destructor. main copies a into b.
scenes.say: User allocates an int and deletes it. Looks careful. Copy a into b. What goes wrong? A double free.
Pause and think. Both objects are destroyed. How many times is the same int deleted?
scenes.q: `User a; User b = a;` raw pointer member. Deletes of the int?

scenes.head: A shallow copy
scenes.say: Twice. We never wrote a copy constructor, so the compiler's copies each member. It copies the pointer, not the int. Two objects now own one int. At the end, b is destroyed and deletes it. Then a deletes the same address again. A double delete, and glibc, the C library's allocator, aborts.

scenes.head: Fix one: the Rule of Three
scenes.say: The classic fix is the Rule of Three. A class that needs a destructor needs a copy constructor and copy assignment too. The copy constructor allocates its own int, a deep copy. Assignment copies the value into the int it owns. Now each deletes its own.

scenes.head: Fix two: own nothing raw
scenes.say: Even better: avoid it. Here a plain int does the job, and the compiler's copy is correct. That's the Rule of Zero. If you truly need the heap, use unique pointer. Then the accidental copy won't compile. A compile error beats a crash.

panels.label: Rule of Zero
unique_ptr

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Returning a local's address? The local dies at return, so the pointer dangles. Fix? Return by value, or unique pointer.
rows: `x` dies at return: the pointer dangles

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: New, delete, dereference? Use after free: undefined, even if it prints five. Why? Delete frees, but p keeps the address. Prevent? Unique pointer, and Address Sanitizer.
rows: use after free: undefined, even if it prints 5

scenes.say: How many prints? One Constructor, two Destructors. Why? Test b built from a is the silent copy constructor, not assignment. Order? B dies first, then a.
lines: Why? `Test b = a;` is the silent copy constructor
Order? b is destroyed first, then a

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Pointers after a reallocation? They dangle. Why? Elements move to a new block, and the old one is freed. Fix? Reserve first, or keep an index.
rows: no: reallocation invalidates all of them
elements move to a new block; the old is freed

scenes.say: The memory bug? Shallow copy: both destructors delete the same int. Fix one? Rule of Three, a deep copy. Better? Rule of Zero.
lines: The bug? Shallow copy: both delete the same int
Fix one? Rule of Three: deep copy, copy assignment
Better? Rule of Zero: plain or `unique_ptr`

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Do these next, easy to harder. LeetCode seven oh five, Design HashSet, is manual ownership. LeetCode one fifty five, Min Stack, is a vector that grows. LeetCode seven oh seven, Design Linked List, owns nodes you must free.
rows: manual ownership: Rule of Three or Zero
a vector that grows: return values
owning nodes: every new needs a delete

scenes.say: So say this. A pointer to something dead is undefined. Count constructors, and remember the silent copy. A raw owner needs the Rule of Three, or better, the Rule of Zero.
lines: Dead target: local, freed, or moved vector.
Count objects: the copy constructor is silent.
Raw owner? Rule of Three. Better: Rule of Zero.
